title: Boston Globe: ICE Hired Maine Shooting Agent Despite Documented Abuse Allegations and Mental Health Red Flags
excerpt: An investigation by The Boston Globe found that ICE agent David Brouillette, who fatally shot a Colombian work-authorized man in Biddeford, Maine, had a history of documented domestic violence allegations, protective orders requiring him to surrender firearms, and a self-reported severe head injury—yet was hired during the agency's rapid expansion. Former ICE officials said the vetting process appeared to have been curtailed.
content:
On July 24, 2026, The Boston Globe published a detailed investigation into the background of ICE agent David Brouillette, who had been identified by his ex-wife as the officer who fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13, 2026.

Court records revealed a yearslong trail of abuse allegations from two ex-wives, including protective orders that required Brouillette to relinquish his guns. He also reported a severe head injury that he said significantly impaired his cognitive function. Despite these documented red flags, ICE hired him during its massive hiring push.

  • Former ICE officials said the agency's pre-Trump hiring process included interviews with friends, family, neighbors, and associates, and typically took a full year of vetting and training before a new hire hit the streets. That process appeared to have been compressed.
  • ICE said it "evaluates all available information for every applicant," yet never contacted his ex-wives during vetting, the women said.
  • During the rapid hiring surge, ICE was using background evaluations obtained from other federal agencies—meaning Brouillette may have been hired based on a years-old VA evaluation.
  • Brouillette had previously been rejected from a local police department and voluntarily resigned from a state health agency position after seven months.
  • Border czar Tom Homan acknowledged publicly that the vetting "may have failed" in this case.
"Many law enforcement officials, including former ICE executives, say the agency appears to be cutting corners on the hiring front." — Boston Globe
